ana_01.label: 178,749 repair visits, 25 countries, 447 cafes, 12 years
ana_01.content: The merged RepairMonitor dataset has 178,749 rows spanning 2015-04-04 to 2026-08-07, contributed by 447 distinct Repair Cafe branches across 25 countries. Volunteers logged 1,951 distinct kinds_of_product across 14 categories and 8,600 named brands — a long tail dominated by 'Unknown/n.a.' (78,902 rows, 44%) where the volunteer simply could not identify the manufacturer. The two CSVs (repairs.csv: 11 cols, repairs_text.csv: 12 cols) join 1:1 on repair_id.

ana_02.label: 63.1% of all visits end in a successful fix
ana_02.content: Across the 178,749 logged visits, 112,775 (63.09%) were repaired ('yes'), 43,112 (24.12%) failed ('no'), and 22,859 (12.79%) were partially repaired or end-of-life ('half'). Three rows had unusable values. The dataset's headline 63% fix rate sits almost exactly on the Foundation's 2024 benchmark of 62%, and within a percentage point of the Open Repair Alliance's ~60%, suggesting the figure is a stable property of community repair rather than an artefact of one year or platform.

ana_03.label: The dataset is overwhelmingly Dutch — and that bias matters
ana_03.content: The Netherlands alone contributes 90,839 visits (50.8%) and the top three countries — NL, GB, FR — together account for 82.9% of all rows. Country fix rates vary widely: the US logs the highest among large samples at 70.9%, while France sits at just 55.6%. Tiny samples (KR n=23 at 100%, ZA n=13 at 30.8%) are noisy and should be ignored. The Dutch tilt is unsurprising — the movement was founded in Amsterdam in 2009 — but it means any cross-country claim should be made cautiously.

ana_04.label: Textiles are repaired 92% of the time; electronics around half
ana_04.content: Outcomes split sharply by category. Textiles top the league at 92.3% fixed (n=24,412), followed by Tools non-electric at 90.0% and Jewelry at 82.9%. The big-volume electric categories drag the average down: Household appliances electric — the single largest bucket at 70,983 visits — fixes only 55.3% of the time, Display & sound equipment 45.8%, and Computer equipment / phones 46.4%. Bicycles (81.7%) and non-electric household items (81.4%) sit comfortably in between. The pattern is mechanical-versus-electronic in disguise.

ana_05.label: Easiest products to fix: knives, trousers, shears (>95%); hardest: TVs, milk frothers, video recorders (~30%)
ana_05.content: Restricting to products with at least 500 visits (73 product types), the easiest items to fix are nearly all textile or hand-tool: knives/scissors 97.5% (n=2,915), T-shirts 96.2%, trousers 96.0%, blouses 95.6%, garden shears 95.4%. The hardest are screen and small-kitchen electrics: televisions 29.7% (n=1,293), milk frothers 30.4%, video recorders 31.6%, printers 36.8%, handheld vacuums 37.3%, electric kettles 39.9%. The gap between best and worst is roughly 70 percentage points — far larger than any country-level variation.

ana_06.label: Repair counts grew 4.2x from 2019 to 2025; 2020-21 was the COVID dip
ana_06.content: Annual logged visits climbed from 28 in the 2015 launch year to 15,491 in 2019, dipped sharply during COVID (6,686 in 2020 and 5,813 in 2021 — together less than half of 2019), then surged back to 15,096 in 2022, 29,406 in 2023, 39,981 in 2024 and 45,165 in 2025 (2026 partial: 7,346 through August). That's a 4.2x increase from pre-pandemic 2019 to 2025. The fix rate, by contrast, has been remarkably steady: 60–66% every year since 2017, with 2025 ticking up to 65.5%.

ana_07.label: Top failure reasons: 'no way to fix' (21%), 'spare parts not at session' (18%), 'unidentified failure' (14%)
ana_07.content: Among the 26,537 failed-or-partial visits with a non-null failure_reasons field, the leading reasons are: 'No way to fix the product' (5,544 mentions, 20.9%), 'Spare parts not available at repair session' (4,694, 17.7%), 'Unidentified failure' (3,662, 13.8%), 'Too worn out' (3,341, 12.6%) and 'No way to open the product' (2,305, 8.7%). Combine the three spare-parts buckets (at session, on market, too expensive) and parts availability accounts for 9,042 mentions — 34.1% — making it by far the dominant single barrier. This is exactly the lever the 2024 EU Right to Repair Directive targets.

ana_08.label: GenAI mentions in info-source field grew from 0 to 32 between 2022 and 2026 — but YouTube still leads ~17:1
ana_08.content: Across the small slice of rows where volunteers actually wrote down a repair information source (n=7,191, just 4% of the dataset), YouTube dominates with 879 mentions, followed by 'manual / handleiding / Bedienungsanleitung' (385), Google search (279), iFixit (112) and forums (64). GenAI tools — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Perplexity, Bing Chat — appear 32 times total: zero before 2023, then 3 in 2023, 10 in 2024, 17 in 2025, and 2 in 2026 (partial year). The growth curve is unmistakable, but the absolute share is still tiny: in 2025 YouTube outpaces GenAI by 239 to 17, a 14:1 ratio. Direct answer to TidyTuesday's prompt: GenAI is rising fast, but YouTube has not been overtaken.

ana_09.label: Volunteer-rated repairability tracks outcome almost monotonically (1=14% fixed, 10=86% fixed)
ana_09.content: Volunteers fill in a 1-10 'repairability' score after each visit (non-missing in 124,864 rows, 69.9%). The mean score is 6.66 and median 7. Fix rate climbs almost monotonically with the score: 13.7% at score 1, 34.7% at 2, 48.0% at 3, 56.9% at 5, 70.4% at 7, 78.4% at 8, 84.9% at 9 and 85.8% at 10. Mean score for fixed items is 7.45, vs 4.41 for not-fixed. The strong correlation suggests the score is more a retrospective summary of the visit than an independent property of the device — exactly the caveat raised in det_07.

ana_10.label: Median item brought in is 8 years old; older items are slightly MORE likely to be fixed
ana_10.content: Where production year is reported (n=64,025, 35.8%), the median estimated year of production is 2014 and the mean 2007.7. Implied age-at-repair has a median of 8 years and mean 13.8 years. Counterintuitively, fix rate inches UP with age: 0–4 years 59.5%, 10–14 years 57.0%, 25–29 years 60.2%, 50+ years 63.4%. The gradient is mild (~4 pp from youngest to oldest bucket), but it suggests the very newest items skew toward unrepairable categories (TVs, printers, computer kit) while older items skew toward textiles, mechanical tools, and furniture — consistent with the category-level pattern in ana_04.

ana_11.label: Brand fix rates span 34% (Canon) to 87% (Batavus), but 'Unknown' is 44% of all rows
ana_11.content: Among the 57 brands with at least 300 logged visits, the worst fix rates are Canon 34.1% (n=839), LG 35.3%, Bose 36.3%, JVC 39.2%, Nespresso 41.9%, Samsung 42.5%, Panasonic 42.7%. The best are bicycle brands and mechanical-textile brands: Batavus 86.5% (n=318), Gazelle 83.6%, Pfaff (sewing) 73.8%, Singer (sewing) 67.3%, Ikea 66.5%, Miele 65.6%. Major appliance brand Philips, the largest named bucket at 10,649 visits, fixes 54.4%. The single biggest 'brand' bucket is 'Unknown/n.a.' at 78,902 rows (44% of all data), with a 73.9% fix rate — its own composition (heavy in textiles and bicycles where the brand is not on the label) explains the high score.

ana_12.label: Spare parts dominate failures most in electrical tools (17.8% combined) and household electrics (12.5%)
ana_12.content: Cross-tabulating top categories against the three spare-parts failure buckets shows the regulation-relevant pattern. For electrical tools (4,755 failed visits), 8.16% cite 'parts not at session', 3.91% 'parts not on market', 5.70% 'parts too expensive' — combined 17.8%. For household electric appliances (31,754 failed), the combined parts share is 16.4% (8.0 + 4.1 + 4.3). Display & sound is 11.6%. Textiles, by contrast, almost never fail for parts: combined under 1%. The free-text bucket 'Unidentified failure' is highest in display & sound (8.9%), implying diagnostic complexity. These are the slices the EU directive's spare-parts rule is best positioned to move.

ana_13.label: Estimated 1,545 tonnes of CO2 avoided by successful electric repairs (range 644-2,575 t)
ana_13.content: Of the 112,775 successful repairs, 64,369 were in electrical or electronic categories (household electric appliances, display & sound, electric tools, computer/phone, electric toys, clocks). Applying the Restart Project's class-weighted estimate of ~24 kg CO2-equivalent avoided per fixed electric/electronic item gives 1,545 tonnes of CO2e prevented over the 11-year window — equivalent to roughly 335 average European households' annual electricity emissions. Using the 10–40 kg/repair range gives 644–2,575 tonnes. The estimate ignores textiles, bicycles, jewelry and furniture, which together add another 36,500 successful repairs whose carbon savings are real but harder to value with a single multiplier.
